Field surveys indicate that the onset of reproductive maturity is marked by a shell length at puberty of 1.9 centimeters [Lp = 1.9 centimeters], suggesting that individuals invest considerable post-settlement growth before allocating resources to gametogenesis. The wet weight at birth for newly hatched juveniles is approximately 0.000007 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000007 grams], a minuscule mass derived from an egg diameter of roughly 240 micrometers, reflecting the extreme maternal economy typical of species that produce large numbers of small, encapsulated offspring. This initial mass contrasts sharply with the ultimate wet weight of 7 grams [Wwi = 7 grams] attained by fully grown adults, representing a mass increase of six orders of magnitude over the course of somatic development.

The rate is among the highest recorded for any buccinoid neogastropod studied at this temperature, underscoring the species' capacity for rapid population turnover when environmental conditions are favorable.

This extended lifespan is notable among gastropods of comparable adult size, suggesting that Olivancillaria deshayesiana follows a relatively slow-paced life-history strategy despite its moderately high reproductive output. Such a proportional schedule is consistent with theoretical expectations for species that experience low juvenile mortality and stable adult feeding conditions on temperate sandflats.

The volumetric growth trajectory from the 0.000007 gram hatchling to the 7 gram adult involves a dramatic allometric shift in body composition and metabolic demand. Newly settled juveniles begin life feeding on microscopic algae and organic detritus, gradually transitioning to a diet of small bivalves and carrion as the shell length surpasses 1.9 centimeters.
